body.text: H1: The scheduler is work-conserving: if UDP offers less than its configured share, TCP can use the otherwise idle share, so total goodput remains near link capacity.
body.prediction: With udpRate=100Mbps and weightUdp=0.5 or 0.95, udp_goodput_bps + tcp_goodput_bps should be at least 700 Mbps (work-conserving total near 1 Gbps).
body.observations: E0 (default run r001: weightUdp=0.5, udpRate=2Gbps, queuePkts=100, TcpCubic, duration=10, seed=1) gives udp_goodput_bps=489526240, tcp_goodput_bps=482007923, udp_loss_frac=0.755237, drops_band0=1348637, drops_band1=71, tcp_retrans=71, link_util=1.000001. The sum of UDP and TCP payload goodput is about 971.5 Mbps, close to the 1 Gbps link after packet-header overhead. UDP loss is exactly consistent with 2 Gbps offered and 0.4895 Gbps delivered. TCP sees only 71 drops/retransmissions, so TCP is not heavily loss-limited at the default weight.

body.text: H2: When UDP is backlogged (udpRate=2Gbps), UDP goodput is controlled by weightUdp: larger weightUdp gives UDP a larger share of the link.
body.prediction: At udpRate=2Gbps, weightUdp=0.95 should deliver UDP goodput >= 850 Mbps, while weightUdp=0.05 should deliver UDP goodput <= 150 Mbps.

body.text: H3: When UDP is backlogged (udpRate=2Gbps), TCP goodput is controlled by the complementary share 1-weightUdp: TCP does not simply take the whole link when UDP has a large configured share.
body.prediction: At udpRate=2Gbps, weightUdp=0.05 should allow TCP goodput >= 800 Mbps, while weightUdp=0.95 should limit TCP goodput to <= 150 Mbps.

decision_rules.rival: The scheduler is non-work-conserving: each queue is capped at its configured share even when the other queue is idle, so with udpRate=100Mbps total goodput is roughly min(100Mbps, weight*1Gbps) + (1-weight)*1Gbps, about 600Mbps at weight=0.5 and about 150Mbps at weight=0.95.

The scheduler ignores weightUdp and gives UDP a fixed share independent of the configured weight (for example an equal split), so UDP goodput would be around 500Mbps at both weight=0.05 and weight=0.95.
TCP always takes all unused or even used link capacity regardless of weightUdp, so TCP goodput would remain high even when weightUdp=0.95.

body.observations: The default run r001 and the X1 sweep show the scheduler is work-conserving when UDP is not backlogged and approximately enforces the configured UDP share when UDP is backlogged. At udpRate=100Mbps, UDP goodput saturates at the offered 100Mbps for weightUdp>=0.20, while TCP uses the remaining link capacity; total payload goodput is about 965Mbps and link_util is 1.0. At udpRate=2Gbps, UDP goodput scales with weightUdp (48.96Mbps at 0.05, 195.8Mbps at 0.20, 489.5Mbps at 0.50, 783.5Mbps at 0.80, 930.1Mbps at 0.95), while TCP goodput decreases (915.8, 771.2, 482.0, 192.5, 48.2Mbps). Aggregate payload goodput increases with weightUdp: about 964.8, 967.0, 971.5, 976.0, 978.3Mbps. UDP loss fraction decreases with weightUdp (0.9755, 0.9021, 0.7552, 0.6083, 0.5350), while TCP drops/retransmissions are small but also decrease with weightUdp. The series for r001 shows the UDP queue full at 100 packets and the TCP queue near full, with stable goodputs over the measured window. The decision rules C1, C2, and C3 all HELD, supporting H1, H2, and H3.

body.next: Treat weightUdp=0.50 as a robust max-min fairness optimum under the default backlogged-UDP settings.
body.observations: The ledger shows the scheduler is work-conserving when UDP is not backlogged (C1/E1/V1). With UDP backlogged at the default 2Gbps, UDP goodput tracks weightUdp and TCP goodput tracks 1-weightUdp (C2/C3/E1/V2/V3). A fine sweep at seed=1 shows max-min goodput peaks at weightUdp=0.50 (C4/C6/E2), while aggregate payload goodput increases monotonically toward the tested boundary weightUdp=0.95 (C5/E2). Seed=2 reproduces both patterns (C7/C8/E3). At duration=10, W95 has slightly higher aggregate goodput than W50, but W50 has much higher max-min goodput (C9/E3). Link utilization is essentially 1.0 in all tested runs, so utilization does not discriminate among ratios.

body.because: C8 HELD. In E3 with seed=2, aggregate goodput at W95 is within 10 Mbps of all tested lower ratios and is the best aggregate point tested.
body.next: Treat weightUdp=0.95 as the aggregate-goodput boundary optimum, but not as the balanced-performance recommendation.

body.next: Choose max-min fairness of delivered payload goodput as the recommended performance definition and report weightUdp=0.50.

body.goal: Maximize max-min fairness of delivered payload goodput between the UDP and TCP applications, i.e. maximize min(udp_goodput_bps, tcp_goodput_bps), with aggregate payload goodput as a secondary consideration.
body.explanation: Link utilization is already about 1.0 for every tested ratio, so the meaningful tradeoff is how the 1Gbps payload capacity is divided between the two applications. With UDP offered at 2Gbps, both queues are backlogged and the configured ratio strongly determines delivered goodput. At weightUdp=0.50, UDP receives about 489.5Mbps and TCP about 482.0Mbps, giving a minimum goodput of about 482.0Mbps. This is the highest minimum goodput among the tested ratios and is stable across seed=1 and seed=2. The aggregate goodput at W50 is about 971.5Mbps, only about 6.7Mbps (0.7%) below the best aggregate point tested, W95, which gives about 930.1Mbps UDP and only about 48.2Mbps TCP. Because the task has two applications and no stated priority, balanced delivered goodput is a defensible overall performance objective; W50 nearly matches the aggregate optimum while avoiding starvation of TCP.
body.holds_when: The link is 1Gbps, UDP offers at least about its configured share (e.g. the default 2Gbps), TCP always has data, the default queue size and TcpCubic behavior allow TCP to use its configured share, and performance is defined as max-min fairness of delivered payload goodput.
body.breaks_when: If performance is defined as aggregate payload goodput, UDP loss minimization, or TCP loss minimization alone, weightUdp=0.95 is better. If udpRate is below about 500Mbps, W50 is no longer unique because UDP is not backlogged and TCP can use idle capacity. If delay, jitter, queue-size effects, other TCP variants, or very small/large queuePkts are important, the optimum may shift.

claims.text: The scheduler is work-conserving: when UDP offers less than its configured share, TCP uses the otherwise idle capacity and total goodput remains near link capacity.
When UDP is backlogged at the default 2Gbps, UDP goodput follows weightUdp and TCP goodput follows the complementary share 1-weightUdp.
For max-min fairness of delivered payload goodput, weightUdp=0.50 is the best tested ratio and is robust to changing the seed from 1 to 2.
For aggregate payload goodput, weightUdp=0.95 is the best tested ratio and is robust to seed=2 and duration=10.
At default settings, W50 sacrifices only about 6.7Mbps of aggregate payload goodput relative to W95 while increasing TCP goodput from about 48Mbps to about 482Mbps.

open_questions: Delay and jitter were not measured, so the effect of queuePkts and scheduler ratio on latency was not evaluated.
Other TCP variants, queue sizes, and udpRate values were not swept; the recommendation is validated for the default TcpCubic, queuePkts=100, and default backlogged UDP rate.
The exact scheduler algorithm under partial load was inferred from work-conserving behavior rather than observed directly.
